profile.story: Grace Liu left a regional firm in 2012 and built a ten-person practice in Bellevue serving closely-held businesses and their owners — tax compliance, monthly accounting, payroll and a growing advisory line. $1.61M of revenue, 58% of it earned between January and April. The firm is unusually well documented for its size: Karbon templates for every engagement, refreshed each August, and a review checklist the reviewing partner actually signs. It has also gone further with AI than most firms twice its size — inbound client documents are classified automatically and letters are drafted against a written policy. What has not moved is the fee schedule, dated January 2023, and the season inbox, where 42% of inquiries never get a call back.

blockNotes.b1: Grace's stated bottleneck is March capacity. She said it three times. Objective is growth, but the outcomes she wrote in q4 are all about intake and realization, not about doing more returns — worth showing her that her own targets disagree with her diagnosis.
blockNotes.b2: 208 inquiries a year, all captured in Karbon, and that is exactly why the leak is measurable: Robin pulled the season log and 61 of 136 January–April inquiries have no outbound activity of any kind. Off-season is fine. Funnel reconciles: 208 × 46% × $2,400 = ~$230K of new fees against 91% retention on a $1.61M base — pass.
blockNotes.b3: Best-documented small firm we have scored. Karbon templates for all ten workflows, refreshed each August, and the review checklist is signed on every file — we opened four at random and all four were complete. This is a genuine 4 on S5 and we should say so plainly.
blockNotes.b4: 24.7 h/wk of repetitive work across ten people, 14.6 of it document chasing during season. Against ~380 available hours that is 6.5% — pass. The chasing is seasonal: it is 18 weeks of the year, not 52, and the calculator is built that way.
blockNotes.b5: Daniel walked us through the AI stack: a document classifier on inbound portal uploads, and first-draft letters. There is a written policy — we read it — naming who reviews, what data may not go near a public model, and who owns each implementation. Measurement is the gap: nobody can say what the classifier saved. Largest client 11%, contracts written, no legal exposure. Backups are the only hygiene flag.

P1.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs volume at least roughly tracked; Karbon logs the inquiry but nobody counts by source.

P2.note: Every inquiry is captured in Karbon — the capture is good. The response is not: the season log pulled live shows 61 of 136 January–April inquiries with no outbound activity at all, and q24 says 'nobody owns getting back to them'.
P2.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs inquiries usually answered within a day; for four months of the year 45% are never answered.

P3.note: q24: off-season most inquiries get a second touch, 'in season, almost none'. There is no sequence — it depends on whether Grace or Daniel remembers the name.
P3.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs follow-up that happens across most leads even if person-dependent; for the four months that produce 58% of revenue it does not happen.

P4.note: q25: ~46% close 'of the ones we actually respond to', not tracked by source or person, and 'Daniel and I each do it our own way'. Loss reason recorded anecdotally as slow response then fee.
P4.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs a loose process and a rate roughly tracked; the rate is a partner's impression and the denominator excludes everyone never called back.

P5.note: Fee schedule footer dated January 2023 (Doc). One across-the-board 3% move since, applied in 2024 without a cost basis. Realization report shows the compliance book at 78%. q28: 'Unchanged for 2+ years' and 'Pricing is a current worry'; Daniel wants to move faster than Grace does (q9).
P5.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs real economics behind prices and occasional reviews; the realization data exists and has never been used to reset a fee.

P6.note: q29: CAS and planning are 'mentioned at the year-end meeting when there is time'. Advisory is the highest-margin line at 71% and the smallest at 14%. No bundles, no named packages, no scripted upsell.
P6.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs named tiers or bundles and a scripted upsell on the core offer; the advisory retainer exists but has never been named or packaged.

P7.note: Karbon retention view shown live: 91% return the following season, CAS retainers at 94%. Robin runs a did-not-return list every May and an extension list every September, and both were worked last year.
P7.why_not_higher: Anchor 4 needs retention worked on a cadence with reactivation measured; the two campaigns run but nobody reports what they recovered.

P8.note: q30: marketing is 'me, in July and August', sales is the two partners, budget $750/mo, and leads, conversion, CAC and value are never reviewed together — only fee per client, once a year in August.
P8.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs named owners and numbers reviewed at least sometimes; marketing has no owner for ten months of the year.

assessment.owner_objective: Reliable revenue growth — grow the advisory line without growing the season, and stop being the only person who can price an engagement.
assessment.owner_belief: Our problem is capacity in March. We cannot take on more clients because the season already breaks us, and every year I promise myself we will fix it in the summer and every summer we are too tired to. It has been like this since about 2019.
assessment.primary_constraint: The firm's intake and pricing both run through one partner's desk in the four months when that desk is fully occupied by review, so new revenue is lost at the door in season and the fees on the work that does come in are set against a 2023 schedule the firm's own realization data contradicts.
assessment.constraint_symptoms: Block 2: 61 of 136 season inquiries have no outbound activity at all, and the top loss reason is 'we took too long to call back'. Block 1: 'nobody else quotes an engagement', and Grace's own q4 targets are intake and realization, not throughput. Block 3: the documented process is excellent — and starts only after someone has become a client. Block 5: fee reasoning is named in q52 as living in Grace's head rather than in Karbon. Four blocks; the rule requires two.
assessment.constraint_cost: ~$53K of expected operating profit a year from inquiries never called back (87 unanswered × 46% close × $2,400 × 55% margin, funnel Doc) · ~$41K of fee realization given away by a January 2023 schedule against a compliance book running at 78% (realization report, Doc) · 263 season hours a year chasing client documents.
assessment.constraint_fix: Separate intake from review. One named owner for every inquiry with a 24-hour callback standard that holds in February, a scoping and fee matrix that lets Daniel and the two managers quote standard engagements without Grace, and a fee schedule rebuilt from the realization report before the January engagement-letter run.
assessment.momentum_initiative: The 24-hour callback rule with Robin as the named owner and a Karbon view that shows any inquiry older than one day in red. It is a decision, not a project, it costs nothing, and it can be measured inside 30 days.

opportunities.title: Answer the inquiries that arrive between January and April
opportunities.finding: The season inquiry log pulled live shows 61 of 136 January–April inquiries with no outbound activity of any kind, and q24 confirms 'nobody owns getting back to them'. Across the year that is 42% of 208 inquiries. The firm's own close rate on the ones it does answer is 46%, and the loss reason it records most often is 'we took too long to call back'. The capture is already perfect — every one of these is sitting in Karbon.
opportunities.blueprint: Robin owns intake with a 24-hour callback standard that does not lapse in February. A Karbon view flags any inquiry older than one day. A two-question qualifying script routes the ones the firm wants to Daniel with a fee from the matrix, and politely declines the rest the same week instead of silently.
opportunities.replaces: A season inbox where 45% of inquiries are never contacted and the decline is delivered by silence.

opportunities.title: Reset the individual-return fees against the firm's own realization data
opportunities.finding: The fee schedule footer reads January 2023 (Doc) and the only move since was a 3% across-the-board increase in 2024 applied without a cost basis. The Karbon realization report (Doc) puts the compliance book at 78% and the individual book — 27% of revenue, all of it delivered inside ten weeks — at the bottom of it. The firm already has the data; it has never been used to set a price.
opportunities.blueprint: Rebuild the individual-return fee bands from realized hours by complexity tier, publish the bands in the January engagement letters, and set a written minimum for the standalone 1040 work the firm says it regrets taking. The volume that walks at a 6% increase is the volume that is already below the minimum.
opportunities.replaces: A three-year-old schedule and an annual across-the-board percentage that treats a 78%-realization engagement the same as a 91% one.

opportunities.title: Take the document chase past the third nudge
opportunities.finding: 14.6 h/wk of season time goes on chasing missing client documents — the largest single line in the repetitive-work inventory, flagged for errors, and the point where the automated ladder deliberately stops and hands the work to a person. It runs for the 18 weeks of the season, not all year, and the calculator is built on 18 weeks.
opportunities.blueprint: Extend the SafeSend and Karbon request ladder to a fourth and fifth touch with escalating channels, drive it from the actual document checklist rather than a generic reminder, and give the client a running 'what is still missing' view instead of a phone call. Recovered admin hours redeploy onto intake callbacks, which is where opportunity one gets its capacity.
opportunities.replaces: A three-step ladder that stops exactly where the work gets hard, and 263 season hours of phone calls.
